summary: Defines an extension to CoAP that lets a client observe a resource: it gets the current state and then receives updates from the server as the state changes. The approach is best-effort and suits constrained devices and networks.

plainLanguage.summary: CoAP Observe lets a client ask for a resource and then receive updated representations from the server. Updates are best-effort, so clients must track their freshness and cannot expect every change.

subtitle: A CoAP client registers once and receives later representations as a resource changes.

tldr.problem: A client that needs a resource's changing state would otherwise have to poll repeatedly, which adds overhead for constrained networks and devices.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends GET with Observe value 0. The server returns the current representation and sends later responses as notifications when the resource changes.
tldr.outcome: Observe provides best-effort updates with eventual consistency, sequence numbers for ordering and Max-Age for freshness. RFC 7641 is updated by RFC 8323.

facts.label: Confirmable notification interval
facts.value: At least every 24 hours when mostly non-confirmable

today: RFC 7641 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2015. It has been updated by RFC 8323.

sections.title: Registering Interest in a Resource
sections.content:
CoAP is a RESTful protocol for constrained nodes and networks. A normal request returns the current representation of a resource, but repeated polling adds work when a client wants updates over time.

RFC 7641 adds an observer mechanism. A client sends an extended GET, and the server keeps an observer entry. The initial response and later notifications contain full resource representations and use the request's token so the client can match them to its request.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can register once and receive further responses from the server when the resource changes. It does not need to ask for the current state again and again.

sections.title: Best-Effort Updates and Freshness
sections.content:
The observed state can differ temporarily from the server's actual state because of delay, lost notifications or a server that removes an observer by mistake. The protocol is best-effort and may skip intermediate states, especially when congestion limits delivery.

Each notification has a Max-Age that says how long its representation may be treated as current. If the resource stops changing, the protocol aims for eventual consistency: registered observers eventually receive its latest state. The server decides which resources are observable and when their state changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Some updates may arrive late or not at all. Max-Age tells the client when it must stop treating a representation as current.

sections.title: The Observe Option
sections.content:
Observe is option number 6. Its unsigned integer value uses zero to three bytes. In a GET request, value 0 registers interest and value 1 removes it. The server records the client endpoint and request token.

In a response, the Observe Option identifies a notification and carries a sequence number for detecting reordering. If the server cannot or will not register the client, it returns a normal GET response without the option; the client then needs another way to obtain updates, such as polling.
sections.plainLanguage: In a request, Observe value 0 means register and 1 means deregister. In a response, the option marks a notification and gives it an ordering number.

sections.title: Notifications and Client Choices
sections.content:
Notifications are additional responses to the original GET and carry the client's token. They normally use response code 2.05 (Content) and the same Content-Format as the first response. If the resource changes so a normal GET would return a non-2.xx response, the server sends that response and removes the observer.

The server assigns a strictly increasing sequence number, represented by the 24 least significant bits. The client uses it with local timing to identify newer notifications. A client can deregister with GET and Observe value 1, or stop recognizing the token so a later notification is rejected.
sections.plainLanguage: Each notification repeats the request token and carries a number that helps the client detect older messages arriving late. The client can explicitly deregister or stop accepting notifications.

sections.title: Transmission, Congestion and Intermediaries
sections.content:
A notification may be confirmable or non-confirmable. A server must limit outstanding notifications to a client to NSTART, which is 1 by default, and SHOULD limit non-confirmable traffic to one per round-trip time on average. If it cannot estimate round-trip time, it SHOULD send no more than one non-confirmable notification every 3 seconds.

A proxy may register upstream once for several clients and fan out notifications locally. Each hop manages its own sequence numbers and Max-Age. A server that mainly sends non-confirmable notifications must send one confirmable notification at least every 24 hours to check that the client remains interested.
sections.plainLanguage: The server limits notification traffic and may skip intermediate states while ensuring observers eventually get the latest state. A proxy can share one upstream observation among several clients.

sections.title: Security and Resource Risks
sections.content:
Observing can amplify traffic because one small request may lead to many larger notifications. Without client authentication, servers MUST limit notifications between acknowledgements and intersperse non-confirmable notifications with confirmable ones.

Clients must not use a representation after Max-Age expires. Servers may restrict creation of observer entries to avoid resource exhaustion, and intermediaries must prevent notification loops. When CoAP uses DTLS, notifications must remain within the same epoch of the same connection as the request.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers need limits because an attacker could use observation requests to trigger many notifications. Clients should not rely on data after its stated freshness period ends.
